name: Beth Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a rural firm with two offices, and I'm in the smaller one in a farming town, five of us next to the cattle market. My clients are farms, a vet practice and a lot of tradespeople, plumbers, roofers, a tree surgeon. I prepare their year-end accounts and tax returns, and I spend a fair bit of time explaining to farmers why their subsidy payment counts as income. I like that I know everyone, from church or my parents' garage. What wears me out is market day, when half my clients drop in without an appointment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you find the technical side, and the tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still learning, honestly. Mrs Doyle, my manager, sends back a lot of my farm files, because farm accounts have their own odd rules about livestock values. I use AI now and then, mostly to tidy up a letter or remind me of a rule, once I've seen the others use it safely. I wouldn't let it near a farmer's numbers on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, back to work. At church or at the garage I'd say people round here never trusted AI much anyway. Our farm clients like a face they know. I'm not much for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. Our clients like a face they know, the work's steady, and my fiancé Jakub's an electrician, so his trade's busy. We've got the wedding next summer in the village church, and about four months saved besides the wedding pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, pass my exams this year, and ask Mrs Doyle to give me more of the farm files so I get better at them. We'd keep saving for the wedding, about two hundred and fifty a month. And I'd keep using the AI for letters, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really, apart from the wedding seating plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in your life that would still worry you in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' garage, a bit. Dad's sixty-two and electric cars need fewer repairs, so his work's slower. But that's been coming for years, it's not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's hard about the seating plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jakub's family is Polish and mine's from round here, and both sides think they're the main event. My gran wants to sit near the vicar. It's a nice kind of problem.

say: I'd say **back to work**, and that locals never trusted it.
I'd say it at **church and the garage**, not online.
think: It **suits me**: clients want a face they know and work's steady.
Jakub's **electrician trade** is busy and we have four months saved.
do: Ask Mrs Doyle for more **farm files** to improve.
Save **£250 a month** for the wedding.
feel: **Calm** and content, apart from the **seating plan**.
S0.quote: People round here never trusted AI much anyway. Our farm clients like a face they know.
fieldNote: Her **local ties** make her feel secure: clients know her from church and the garage.
Her fiancé's **busy trade** adds to the sense of safety.
Her father's garage slowing with **electric cars** is a quiet, older worry.

steps.text: Pass this year's exams and take more farm files
Save £250 a month for the village wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and you adapt like farmers always have with new machines. At work I'd say we should use it where it helps and keep the personal service. I'd probably say it to clients too, so they know we're not going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gets harder for juniors. The bigger office would bring in software that does a farmer's return in minutes, and Mrs Doyle won't need as many of us checking by hand. I'd probably keep my job for a while because the farmers know me, but I'd not get the rises I'd hoped for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever software the firm brings in, once I'd seen the bigger office use it for a few months. I'd start doing Jakub's books for his electrical business properly, evenings, so I've got a second string. And we'd save a bit more, three hundred a month instead of two-fifty, and maybe trim the wedding guest list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frightened. Like watching the weather change on a show day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Jakub's books, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his business is growing and he's hopeless with paperwork, he keeps receipts in the van's glovebox. If my hours get cut, I could run my fiancé's office side, the way my mum does for my dad at the garage. We'd still be one household business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trim the guest list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few, the cousins we've never met. My gran would be upset if we cut the choir. I'd sooner cut the flowers than the choir.

say: I'd say we **adapt** like farmers do with new machines.
I'd tell clients we keep the **personal service**.
think: Software doing farm returns in **minutes** means fewer juniors.
I'd keep my job for a while but **miss the rises** I'd hoped for.
do: Learn the firm's software after the **bigger office** tries it.
Do **Jakub's books** properly in the evenings.
Raise savings to **£300 a month** and trim the guest list.
feel: **Anxious** but not frightened, like weather turning on show day.
S1.quote: If my hours get cut, I could run my fiancé's office side, the way my mum does for my dad at the garage.
fieldNote: She expects **slower pay growth** more than sudden job loss, thanks to local loyalty.
Her fallback copies her **parents' model**: the wife running the business office.
She waits for the **bigger office** to prove tools before adopting them.

steps.text: Learn the new software after the main office tests it
Run the books for Jakub's electrical business
Raise savings from £250 to £300 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and people should be careful who they trust. At church I'd say we'll need each other. I wouldn't go blaming anyone loudly, I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone within the year. AGI would do a farm return and the tax, and the bigger office would close our little one. Jakub's electrical work is hands-on, so he's got till about 2031. I'd be the one depending on my fiancé, which isn't how I imagined it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding forward and make it small, the church and a lunch at the village hall, and keep the money. I'd go into Jakub's business full-time, doing quotes, bookings and the van schedule, at least until AI does that too. And I'd help Dad at the garage, because between the two businesses the family keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick at night, I think. Proud in the day, not showing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI would do the quotes too. So what's your job in Jakub's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Maybe answering the phone to people who want a person, and handing him tools on big jobs. I'd learn some of the trade, I suppose. I haven't thought it through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new car we'd talked about, and the honeymoon abroad. We'd go to the coast for a week instead. I'd put everything into a pot for when the robots come for Jakub too.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and to be careful who you trust.
At church I'd say **we'll need each other**.
think: My **job's gone** within the year as our small office closes.
Jakub's **hands-on work** lasts till about 2031, so I'd depend on him.
do: Move the wedding forward and make it **small**.
Join **Jakub's business** full-time doing quotes and bookings.
Help **Dad at the garage** so the family keeps going.
feel: **Worried sick** at night, proud in the day.
S2.quote: I'd be the one depending on my fiancé, which isn't how I imagined it.
fieldNote: She expects her **job to end** within a year when the small office closes.
When pressed, she admits her role in the **family business** isn't thought through.
She'd save for the day **robots reach** her fiancé's trade too.

steps.text: Hold a small church wedding sooner and keep the savings
Work full-time in Jakub's electrical business
Drop the new car and the honeymoon abroad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and we'd be foolish not to use it. At work I'd suggest we tell clients what's coming. At church I'd say look after the young ones starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd qualify, have a few good years, then expect to leave the firm around 2031. By then I'd want Jakub's business to be big enough for both of us, with the three robot years on top. I'd want to know some of the trade by then, not just the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028, then do an evening course in electrical installation so I can work alongside Jakub. We'd buy a second van together around 2029 and take on bigger jobs, like solar panels on farms. And we'd keep the wedding as planned, it's paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. It feels like a plan we'd make together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people round here accept a woman electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older farmers might raise an eyebrow at a woman electrician, but they'd get over it once the lights worked. My gran ran a dairy on her own after Grandad died. Round here people respect work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose, leaving accounts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The degree, sort of, and the pride of being the first in my family to have one. But I'd still use it, running our business. It wouldn't be wasted.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning**, and we'd be foolish not to use it.
I'd suggest we tell **clients** what's coming and look after the young ones starting out.
think: I'd qualify and expect to **leave the firm** around 2031.
Jakub's business could carry both of us with the **robot years** on top.
do: Qualify by 2028, then take an **electrical installation** course.
Buy a **second van** with Jakub around 2029.
feel: **Anxious but hopeful**, a plan made together.
S3.quote: Some of the older farmers might raise an eyebrow at a woman electrician, but they'd get over it once the lights worked.
fieldNote: Five years lets her plan to **learn the trade**, not just do the paperwork.
Her pride in being the first **graduate in the family** tempers the move.
She leans on **local values**: people respect work, whoever does it.

steps.text: Take an evening course in electrical installation
Buy a second van with Jakub around 2029
Leave the firm for the family business around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people should just keep working and plan sensibly. At work I'd say let's get good at the tools and keep the clients. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine for most of it. I'd qualify, maybe become a senior at the small office, and help Jakub's business grow on the side. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with probably two children, and I'd move into the business then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify and learn the AI tools once the others do. We'd buy a house in the village, with a yard for Jakub's vans. And I'd do his books on the side the whole time, so moving over later is easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. It feels a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With two years I'd wait. With ten years, we'd have children soon after the wedding, and my mum would be the childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Doyle, maybe, she's fifty-five and the firm is her life. And the farmers who don't use computers at all. They'll need someone to explain things, which might be me for a while.

I'd suggest we get good at **the tools** and keep clients.

By 2036 I'd move into **Jakub's business** with two children.
do: Learn the **AI tools** once others do.
Buy a **house in the village** with a yard for vans.

feel: **Uneasy** at most, because it feels a **long way off**.

fieldNote: A decade keeps her **accounting career** intact while a family business grows beside it.
She worries for her **manager** and offline farmers more than herself.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tools after colleagues adopt them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It'd rush the wedding, the job and everything we'd planned into a few months. What would help is support for small family businesses, like Jakub's and my dad's, to take on people, and training that fits around work, evenings, not full-time courses in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the countryside depends on people who know each other. Farmers round here ring me before they ring the tax office, because my dad fixed their tractors. I don't know if AI can earn that.

headlineQuote: Farmers round here ring me before they ring the tax office, because my dad fixed their tractors.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old junior** at a small rural office next to the cattle market.
She uses AI **now and then**, after colleagues show it's safe.
She's marrying Jakub, an **electrician**, and plans her future around their household business.
In faster pictures she'd join **Jakub's business** and even learn the trade.
Her **local ties** and faith shape how she sees work and who she leans on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, rushing the wedding, job and plans into a few months.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **family businesses** to take on people.
**Evening training** that fits around work, not city courses.
